column1: # key() AT GENERATED PATHS (G8 phase 1). The template is cloned per
# destination, so `key()` inside it answers for the destination — which
# is what makes computed names work without string interpolation:
# `"acme/" + key() + ":1.4.2"`. Columns: name<TAB>mode<TAB>src<TAB>expect
# The rows with key() under an operator or a function are the ones that
# earn this file. A key() the bag walk reaches directly is re-pathed by
# its own residuation clone every pass; one nested inside a call is
# not, and answered for the position the TEMPLATE was written at until
# this phase (see KeyFuncVal.resolve, and go/func.go's keyFunc, which
# reach the same answers by different tests — DIVERGENCE.md).

# A TEMPLATE IS APPLIED ONCE, however deep the reference that reaches
# it. `a: b: c: d: e: $.a.b.f` pointing at a bag with `&: {n: key()}`
# used to REFUSE in TypeScript at four levels and answer in Go, while
# two and three levels agreed -- a threshold nobody wrote, which is
# what said it was a defect rather than a divergence (BUGS.md §50).
# Go was right, and these rows are why we can say so: the four-level
# answer is the agreed THREE-level answer with one more level of
# nesting, character for character. The cause was that the bag loops'
# apply-once mark is by template IDENTITY, and every Val takes a fresh
# id when constructed -- so a reference cloning a templated bag cloned
# its template into something the mark could not match, and the
# template was applied a SECOND time over the value the first
# application had produced: `n: key()` had answered "x", the template
# met that string as a map, and the inner key() answered "n".
# The depth ladder is the row set, because the threshold is the defect.
key-spread-through-ref-2
